Choosing renovations with a strong return on investment (ROI) may help increase your home's resale value and build equity. Let's explore some home improvement projects that tend to retain value, along with a few tips for planning your next upgrade.

- The highest-ROI home improvements aren't always the largest or most expensive projects
- Local market conditions and buyer preferences can influence how much value a renovation adds
- Some renovations may increase home equity, while others are worthwhile simply because they improve how you live in your home

Have you been thinking about starting a home renovation project? Before you start knocking down walls or picking out finishes, it's helpful to consider both the project’s cost and the value it may add to your home. Whether you're preparing to sell or planning to stay for years to come, understanding how different renovations can affect your home's value can help you make more informed decisions.


While few improvements recoup every dollar spent, some projects may increase your home's value and contribute to higher equity.[Home equity](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/home-equity-loans-guide) is the difference between your home's market value and the amount you owe on your mortgage. Of course, not every renovation is about resale value or ROI. Some projects are simply about making your home more comfortable, functional or enjoyable.


Homeowners continue to invest heavily in their properties. According to[Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/remodeling-growth-set-downshift-late-2026) , annual spending on home improvements and repairs is expected to exceed $518 billion by the end of 2026, underscoring the ongoing demand for remodeling projects.


## 10 Home Improvements That Add Value


One way to evaluate a remodeling project's potential value is to compare its cost with the amount it may add to your home's resale value. This ROI estimate can help you compare projects and identify upgrades that may offer a higher financial return.


Keep in mind that resale value can vary based on factors such as your local housing market, your home's condition and the quality of the work completed. Also, the projects with the highest ROI aren't always the biggest or most expensive renovations. In many cases, smaller updates can deliver a stronger return than large-scale remodels.

## Pre-Renovation Checklist


Long before you start ripping up floors, you should consider the following:


- Have you budgeted for the renovation costs?
- Is it fixing a problem?
- How long do you plan to live in the home?
- Can you afford the renovation if you don’t recoup the full or significant amount of your investment?
- How long will the renovation last?
- Could the improvements increase your home equity?


Still unsure if your project is worth the cost? Here’s a more in-depth look at the questions above.


### Don’t Guesstimate Your Renovation Budget


Even the most carefully planned renovation can come with additional expenses, so it's important to look beyond the initial estimate. As you evaluate a project's potential value, take time to understand the full scope of costs involved and how they fit within your budget.


A few ways to plan include:


- Get estimates from multiple contractors to compare pricing, timelines and scope of work
- Build a contingency fund into your budget to help cover unexpected expenses
- Prioritize necessary repairs and maintenance before focusing on cosmetic upgrades
- Factor in all project costs, including permits, materials, labor and potential surprises that may arise once work begins


### Prioritize Long-Term Solutions


While your budget will influence the scope of a project, it's important to determine whether you're fixing the underlying issue or applying a temporary solution.


For example, if an upstairs leak has caused mold on the ceiling below, a quick grout repair won't solve it. A professional inspection can help identify the source of the problem and any additional repairs that may be needed. In some cases, addressing the root cause may provide more long-term value than a short-term fix.


### Match Projects to Your Timeline


If you're planning to sell in the near future, focus on improvements that appeal to a broad range of buyers. If you expect to stay in your home for several years, personal preferences and everyday enjoyment may carry more weight.


As you weigh potential projects, think about:


- When you plan to put your home on the market
- Whether the improvement is likely to appeal to a wide buyer pool
- Whether a smaller update could offer a greater return than a major remodel
- How long you will have to enjoy the upgrade before putting your home on the market


### Research Your Project’s Regional ROI


It's important to think about the value of renovations in your region, not just on a national scale. The projects that add value in one market may not have the same impact in another. In colder climates, energy-efficiency upgrades may be especially appealing to buyers, while a[swimming pool](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/make-a-splash-alternatives-to-the-back-yard-pool) could be less desirable. In warmer regions, those preferences may be reversed.


When researching a project, pay attention to:


- Regional climate and buyer preferences
- Features and upgrades commonly found in nearby homes
- Recent neighborhood sales and local housing trends
- Whether the scope of your project aligns with surrounding homes


Neighborhood comps, or recently sold homes with similar features in your area, can help guide your decisions. You can find this information through online real estate listings, local market reports or a real estate agent. For larger projects, a local real estate agent or appraiser can also provide insight into how similar improvements have performed in your area. If your renovation involves an addition or structural changes, be sure to check local permit requirements before work begins.


### Think Beyond Resale Value


Sometimes, home improvement projects are simply about making your home work better for you — and that's OK. While not every renovation will fully recoup its cost, some improvements may increase your home's value and contribute to higher equity.


That added equity can provide future financial flexibility. Depending on your qualifications, you may be able to access a portion of your available equity through a[home equity loan](https://www.pennymac.com/refinancing-products/home-equity-loans) or[cash-out refinance](https://www.pennymac.com/refinancing-products/cash-out-refinance) . Homeowners use these financing options for a variety of purposes, including renovations, education expenses, debt consolidation and other major expenses.


## Remodeling Mistakes to Avoid


When it comes to home improvements, too often homeowners rely on instinct rather than research when deciding which projects to take on. For example, converting a garage into an extra bedroom may seem like a smart way to add living space, but the loss of parking could make the home less appealing to some buyers.


Here are some remodeling mistakes to avoid:


- **Underestimating project costs:** Make sure you understand the full scope of the project, including materials, labor, permits, inspections and any electrical or plumbing work that may be required.
- **Not planning for the unexpected:** Renovations don't always go according to plan. Building a contingency fund into your budget can help cover unforeseen expenses.
- **Choosing overly personalized upgrades:** Highly customized features may suit your tastes, but could have limited appeal to future buyers.
- **Assuming bigger projects deliver bigger returns:** More expensive renovations don't always provide the highest return on investment.
- **Ignoring permits and inspection requirements:** Skipping required approvals can create delays, additional costs and complications down the road.
- **Not researching local resale trends:** Buyer preferences vary by market. Look at comparable homes and recent sales before committing to a major project.
- **Setting unrealistic expectations:** Home renovation shows can make projects look faster, easier and less expensive than they are in reality.


## Home Improvement Cost vs. Value FAQs


### Which Home Renovations Add the Most Value?


The renovations that add the most value can vary by market, climate and buyer preferences. In some areas, projects such as entry door replacements, garage door upgrades, minor[kitchen updates](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/kitchen-remodel-on-a-budget) and energy-efficiency improvements may offer favorable returns.


### What Is Home Improvement ROI?


Home improvement ROI, or return on investment, is an estimate of how a renovation's cost compares with the value it may add to a home. Actual results will vary based on the project, local market conditions and other factors.


### Can Home Improvements Increase Home Equity?


Home improvements may increase home equity if they contribute to a higher home value. However, not all renovations increase value, and the impact of any project will depend on factors such as the improvement itself, local market conditions, and broader housing market trends.


## Make Your Home Improvement Plan


Whether you're a first-time homeowner with a growing family or about to retire and looking to sell and downsize, it's important to understand which home improvement projects make the most sense for you.
